💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that anastasia Sycheva is the founder and art director of Feely Studio, a branding agency for technology startups.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • When a branding project fails, it usually happens long before the logo stage: in the strategy phase, when words like “modern,” “trustworthy,” “premium,” “friendly,” and “disruptive” are left undefined.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that anastasia Sycheva is the founder and art director of Feely Studio, a branding agency for technology startups. Since 2016, she has helped SaaS, fintech, … More about Anastasia ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

When a branding project fails, it usually happens long before the logo stage: in the strategy phase, when words like “modern,” “trustworthy,” “premium,” “friendly,” and “disruptive” are left undefined. The result is a gap between what the brand is supposed to communicate and what the designer is expected to create. This is the space I like to call the “pre-concept” phase.

At the beginning of a project, designers usually receive many inputs: a brief, a few stakeholder conversations, competitor references, maybe a moodboard or a list of adjectives. From there, they are expected to create visual concepts that feel right. But “right” is difficult to judge when the team has not agreed on what the brand is supposed to communicate in the first place.

In a recent development, as an example, a health tech tech giant we worked with stated they wanted to look modern, trustworthy, and disruptive. At first, “disruptive” sounded like a push toward something bold and unconventional. But as we talked, it became clear that disruption, for them, still had to feel credible inside a conservative healthcare environment. Their clients were large government medical institutions. A brand that felt too rebellious, experimental, or visually loud would not create the right kind of trust.

In other words, their version of “disruptive” looked more traditional than the word suggested.

The problem was not that the client used the wrong language. The problem was that the language was too broad to guide design decisions. Before a designer can turn strategy into a visual concept, those words need to become more specific. What kind of modern? Trustworthy in what way? Disruptive compared to whom? And how far can the brand move away from category expectations before it starts to feel wrong for its audience?

Industry observers note that this article is about that pre-concept phase: the work that happens after the kickoff but before the first visual direction. While the broader brand identity process for digital products includes strategy, concepts, implementation, and the assets a product team needs to build consistently, this article focuses on the earlier work that makes the first concept possible: researching the brand context, uncovering hidden assumptions with stakeholders, and turning shared direction into a visual foundation. Rather, a practical bridge between what the brand needs to mean and how it might begin to look.

The first place to build that bridge is the brand workshop, where broad discovery needs to become a clearer understanding of the brand context.

According to recent reports, A brand workshop will naturally cover the standard discovery topics: the business, its goals, the product or service, the competitive landscape, and the target audience. This article will not try to list every question a designer should ask in that workshop. For readers who want a broader starting point, we prepared a Brand Workshop Toolkit: Questions and Exercises, a FigJam framework we use in our studio to structure discovery conversations.

It has been revealed that here, I want to focus on a smaller set of questions that are easy to skip but extremely useful before visual work begins. These questions are less about collecting facts and more about clarifying perception. They help the team understand what the brand needs to make people believe, where it needs to feel credible, and which category assumptions it should follow or challenge.

Perception sits at the center of brand discovery because the brand is shaped in someone else’s mind.

If the brand ultimately lives in someone else’s perception, the workshop has to clarify what perception the team is trying to create.

The perception questions I focus on are:.

These questions help reveal the assumptions behind people’s opinions, instead of simply adding more opinions to the room. The questions matter because brand attributes often sound aligned before they are actually understood. A stakeholder may say the brand should feel “premium,” and everyone may nod. But one person may mean refined and editorial. Another may mean expensive and exclusive. Another may mean clean, quiet, and minimal. The word sounds shared, but it can lead to three completely different visual systems.

For instance, in the health tech project mentioned earlier, the client described the desired brand as “disruptive.” In many categories, that might suggest something bold, loud, or unconventional. But their audience was large government medical institutions, so disruption had to be expressed through clarity, efficiency, and confidence rather than rebellion. If we had taken the word at face value, the visual direction could easily have moved too far from what their audience would trust.

It has been revealed that in another project, a fintech team wanted the brand to feel “bold” without losing credibility. That word created useful tension. The word bold could mean bright colors, oversized typography, and a highly expressive system. But in a financial category, it also had to carry signals of security, control, and competence. The question was not whether the brand should be bold, but what kind of boldness would still feel trustworthy.

Industry observers note that when the team can define what these attributes mean in context, the designer is no longer working from broad adjectives. They are working from a clearer design problem.

Strategically selected questions can uncover part of the verbal layer, but words alone are rarely enough. To move from language into visual direction, it helps to incorporate exercises that make stakeholders think through images, associations, and relative perception.

Jake Knapp makes a similar point in GV’s Three-Hour Brand Sprint:.

The following two exercises help translate what stakeholders say about the brand into material that can later inform look and feel, design principles, and concept development.

This is also where stakeholder participation becomes important. When clients only receive a strategy presentation, they can stay passive. They may agree in the meeting without noticing the assumptions they are bringing into the process. But when they have to place a competitor on a map, choose an image, or explain why a certain reference feels credible, they become active participants. Their attitudes, beliefs, and disagreements become visible before they have a chance to derail the first concept review.

I usually start by looking outward at the category, then inward at the brand itself.

Recent findings suggest that before the workshop, collect screenshots of competitor brands, websites, product interfaces, social visuals, or other visible brand touchpoints. During the workshop, ask the client team to place those competitors on a simple two-axis map.

This exercise is not about deciding which competitors have “good” or “bad” design. It is about understanding how the client reads the category: what feels credible, what feels generic, what feels too conservative, what feels too experimental, and where there may be an open visual territory for the brand.

The axes should be chosen based on the tension the brand needs to solve. For example:.

Industry observers note that for a health tech firm that wants to feel innovative but works with conservative medical institutions, the map might use traditional to progressive and corporate to human. For a fintech brand that wants to stand out without losing trust, it might use understated to bold and accessible to exclusive.

Industry observers note that the most useful part of this exercise is often not the final map, but the disagreement it creates. One stakeholder may read a competitor as progressive, while another sees it as generic. One may see a brand as premium, while another reads it as cold. These disagreements reveal how different people define trust, innovation, credibility, and differentiation. That is exactly the kind of ambiguity that needs to be resolved before design begins.

After the team has discussed the category, I like to turn the conversation inward. One exercise we use for this is called Visual Brand Driver. Each stakeholder is asked to choose images for a set of unrelated categories: transport, typeface, activity, furniture, mood, object, animal, architecture, and drink.

The instruction is key: the images should not represent the person’s personal taste. They should represent the company.

It has been revealed that for example, if the firm were a type of transport, what would it be? A quiet electric car, a high-speed train, a private jet, a bicycle, a delivery van? If it were a piece of furniture, would it be a soft lounge chair, a precise modular desk, or a heavy boardroom table?

After choosing the images, each person adds four or five adjectives to explain why they selected them. This part matters more than the image itself. The same object can mean different things to different people. A train might suggest speed, structure, reliability, mass accessibility, or a fixed route. A lounge chair might suggest comfort, calm, informality, or lack of urgency.

The exercise helps create a deeper layer of brand perception. Instead of asking people to describe the firm directly, it asks them to think through metaphor and association. Patterns and contradictions become visible. One stakeholder may see the brand as refined and calm, another as energetic and experimental. One may describe the company as precise and structured, another as warm and flexible.

According to recent reports, those differences are not a problem. They are useful materials. They show what needs to be clarified before the visual concept phase begins.

In a recent development, this exercise is also helpful because it separates brand perception from aesthetic preference. A stakeholder may personally like a certain image, but if it does not describe the organization, it should not be part of the exercise. That distinction is vital throughout the branding process. The question is not “Do we like this?” but “Does this express the right thing about the brand?”.

Once the workshop has revealed the main assumptions, the next client meeting can turn that shared understanding into a visual foundation. This is still not the first identity concept. It is a working layer between strategy and design, where the client can react to perception, visual principles, and early asset directions before the designer invests time in full concepts.

We usually structure this meeting around three connected layers:.

Together, these layers move the conversation from perception to practical design boundaries.

According to recent reports, look and feel boards are not collections of visuals the team likes. They are perception boards. The designer collects references based on the workshop: desired perception, category tension, competitor codes, stakeholder disagreements, and brand character.

If the brand needs to feel trustworthy, modern, and human, the board should help the team discuss what kind of trust, modernity, and humanity are appropriate. Is the brand calm and institutional, or warm and accessible? Is it progressive through precision, or through a more expressive editorial tone?

The point is to let the client respond to perception before reacting to a logo, color palette, or finished visual system.

Design code makes the direction more specific by translating key brand ideas into visual principles.

Industry observers note that for a parenting app in Germany, personalized support for your unique journey might become organic shapes, handwritten lines, and softer compositions. Parenting is messy and magical might become soft gradients, layered imagery, and playful irregularity. Research-backed support for real life might introduce doctor calls, data snapshots, infographics, and editorial layouts that make the brand feel credible.

For a PR agency working with prop tech companies, momentum in motion might become lines, arrows, ripple effects, or motion blur. Springboard might become a lift-off moment and elastic visual energy. Building blocks might become modular shapes or stacked compositions.

The team is not choosing the final graphic expression here. It is testing whether the visual metaphors make sense before concept design begins.

The final layer brings the conversation down to the building blocks of identity: typography, color, logo style, photography, illustration, and graphic language.

At this stage, the team can discuss questions such as:.

Sources indicate that this gives the designer boundaries without making the final identity predictable. The next step is still concept design, but the team is no longer starting from vague adjectives or private expectations.

Recent findings suggest that before moving into the first concept, it helps to pause and check whether the team has enough shared direction. The checklist is not meant to make every decision in advance. It is meant to make sure the designer is not starting from vague words, hidden assumptions, or unresolved disagreements.

Before creating the first concept, check whether the team has:.

This last point is especially useful. A strong pre-concept phase not only tells the designer what to explore. It also clarifies what to avoid: directions that would be too expected, too cold, too playful, too conservative, too loud, too generic, or too far from what the audience can trust.

When the team can name those boundaries, the first concept becomes easier to evaluate. The conversation shifts from “I like it” or “I do not like it” to “Does this express the brand we agreed on?”.

Recent findings suggest that the first concept should not feel like a guess or a surprise reveal. It should feel like the next step in a direction the team already understands.

In a recent development, that does not mean removing intuition, experimentation, or creative risk from the branding process. It means giving those things a sharper problem to solve. When the team has clarified the brand character, tested visual perception, translated ideas into design principles, and discussed the early building blocks of the identity, the designer can explore with more confidence.

It has been revealed that pre-concept work does not need to make the final identity predictable. It needs to make the conversation around it more meaningful. Instead of asking whether the work matches someone’s private expectation, the team can ask a better question: Does this visual direction express what the brand needs to become?

Nine canary-yellow boxes form a tight grid in the opening frame, and only a tiny red stamp in the lower-right corner tells two Mediterranean harvests apart. Everything else stays locked. Olearius began with a single olive grove purchased in Sardinia before growing into a French oil merchantâs house selecting small-batch harvests across the Mediterranean, starting with Sardinian Semidana and ProvenÃ§al Aglandau. Joining in the summer of 2024, vrai studio carried the project from naming through final production files. Drawn from the Latin oleum and the trade suffix -arius, the name translates literally to oil merchant, and the bottle silhouette follows suit. Working directly with a glassmaker, the studio traded tall cylindrical bottles for a dark, flat, rounded 50 cl flask.

Sources indicate that thereâs nothing on the broad front face of the dark glass except the gold OLEARIUS wordmark, anchored by an arched crossbar inside its A. All harvest data moves to the narrow curved spine. Along that spine, vertical gold lettering pairs flared serif varietal caps with exact grove coordinates â 43Â°51'29.2" N, 8Â°6'5.4" E for Aglandau in Provence, and 9Â°55'29.5" N, 8Â°26'52.5" E for Semidana in Sardinia. Each oil also gets its own monogram variation. On both the glass spine and the stamped black stopper tops, Provence wears a stippled ring of gold dots around the central four-lobed rosette, while Sardinia radiates sharp linear rays. This packaging design turns provenance into crisp typographic coordinates.

Outer cartons push that discipline even further. Across the yellow corrugated board, a blind-embossed band of angled chevrons cuts horizontally beneath the grey logotype. That recessed channel isnât just surface texture. It guides a black closure ribbon printed with tiny gold rosettes, which pulls away to reveal black interior flutes lined in a repeating gold diamond pattern. A wraparound side seal logs the grower and 200-bottle batch count, while a matching yellow paper bag with ribbon handles and studio still lifes on travertine stone complete the packaging design. One red corner mark separates Sardinia from Provence, and the flask doesnât need a paper label at all.

#45993. Tech Report: No, People Don’t Want More AI In Their Life

📅 2026-07-15 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1210 w)

Tech Report: No, People Don’t Want More AI In Their Life

📅 2026-07-15 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1210 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • It has been revealed that many companies silently assume that everybody wants more AI in their lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vitaly Friedman loves beautiful content and doesn’t like to give in easily. When he is not writing, he’s most probably running front-end & UX … More about Vitaly ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

It has been revealed that many companies silently assume that everybody wants more AI in their lives. That people are craving new AI features, new AI products, new AI workflows — that would all magically replace all existing outdated practices and broken ways of working.

Recent findings suggest that but in reality, it seems like people don’t want more AI at all — at least not in the way most AI leaders envision it. Unsurprisingly, many AI features have low adoption and retention — at a very high cost of delivery, and a high risk of reputation damage.

It’s remarkably difficult to make a strong argument with senior leadership, but AI is not a value proposition. New AI features don’t magically make for happy or excited customers. Because AI features are often bolt-ons and separate tools for employees to use, they typically take people out of their regular way of working.

AI is pretty good at amplifying shortcuts and shortcomings in organizations — from data quality to decision making. It can’t magically fix years of accumulated quick patches, technical debt, broken culture and internal politics. If anything, they become more visible with AI as inconsistencies or conflicting priorities and get handed directly to users, who are then left to make sense of the mess themselves.

Because in most organizations, work typically requires hopping on and off between plenty of disconnected and fragmented systems, with a new AI tool, they now have yet another system that they also need to hop on and off. Often it produces more work, and typically it’s not particularly rewarding work either.

On top of that, people are very much aware of the cost of finding and fixing AI hallucinations. Asking AI to generate a response might feel easier than writing from scratch, but it has a cost:.

In a recent development, for many people, AI isn’t something they can proactively choose and explore on their own — it arrives uninvited, at someone else’s pace. On top of that, plenty of messages amplify fears and worries about AI replacing work — so it’s hardly surprising that the perception of AI isn’t excitement. It’s resistance to change and deep anxiety about one’s place in a world that seems to be changing without them.

Sources indicate that at best, AI features might be silently accepted or nodded away. At worst, AI raises concerns, doubts, caution — and calls for a healthy dose of skepticism. And sometimes it’s perceived as a threat or liability — because unlike other features, AI is neither predictable nor reliable.

People don’t dream of AI art museums or AI fridges or AI hotel reception or AI-narrated children’s books. They don’t want their children to have romantic AI partners. Most people don’t want to actively manage (and clean up after) a swarm of AI agents roaming in their bank accounts and acting on their behalf in the real world. And most notably, people don’t really want a magical box to speak to or type into all the time.

Recent findings suggest that I’m always puzzled by the comparison of AI features with how unreliable humans are. But people don’t compare software with other people. They compare features with features — and if one feature in one product is unreliable, while a similar feature works flawlessly in another, they choose the latter. It’s not about AI or not AI, but rather what works consistently and reliably, and what doesn’t.

In a recent development, many conversations about AI are conversations about the speed of delivery. But to many people, there is little value in increasing the speed of delivery. They want to do things well, with enough time to think and make good decisions. They also want to enjoy the time they spend working on things, rather than just ship faster. There is an enormous feeling of reward and achievement that slowly disappears, one vibe-coded change at a time.

People don’t change much. And after all these years, they (still) want features that are fast, accessible, reliable, predictable and useful — every single time. And ideally not the ones that replace their entire workflow, but that augment their way of working — and that take over the most mundane, annoying, and boring tasks that they find no pleasure in.

Industry observers note that many jobs are exposed to AI automation, but in many of them there is a rewarding, unique, creative part that requires taste, point of view, and perhaps even human intuition. And if AI automates boring parts of it, that’s an advantage for everyone. That’s also what enhances productivity and brings more joy in daily life.

According to recent reports, when AI automates tedious and mentally exhausting tasks, its value is much easier to grasp. But for that, AI shouldn’t feel like a bolt-on. It should be deeply integrated into people’s existing workflows. It must also match existing mental models that they have developed and fine-tuned for years or decades. AI should adapt to how people think and make decisions, not the other way around.

According to recent reports, and it doesn’t really matter if these features are branded as “AI”, “smart” or “automation”. However, they must work well for people using them. And that means that people must be aware of use cases where it actually helps them, and be inspired to find more use cases on their own.

Sources indicate that ironically, tools that work well there aren’t “AI-first” — they are “AI-second”. Subtle, humble, calm, ambient, taking a supportive role in the background for work that otherwise is remarkably dull and unnecessary.

According to recent reports, perhaps I’m missing a bigger picture, and perhaps I’m just old school — but I really do like people. Their stories, their thinking, their emotions, their enthusiasm, their laughing. AI can be remarkably helpful in many situations, but so are people. And between the two, I would favor spending time with a human — however imperfect they are — every single time.

In a recent development, no, people don’t need more AI in their lives — they need AI to automate all the boring stuff they have to deal with every day, so they have more time and headspace to do things that they actually love and enjoy doing. That doesn’t mean spending more time with AI — but spending more time with people they love.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans.
  • It has been revealed that “It’s key to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October.
  • The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

October’s Paris art week had become the must-attend fixture of the international art market calendar, particularly for wealthy Americans. No other city could match the range and quality of the French capital’s art fairs and exhibitions, both at public museums and private foundations. And what about all those charming restaurants, cafes and shops?

It has been revealed that “It’s key to be in Paris,” said Chris Sharp, the Los Angeles gallerist and founder of Post-Fair, a boutique California-based event that held its first edition in the French capital this October. “Paris is the undisputed capital of the art world—once a year,” Sharp added, speaking at Post-Fair’s preview on 19 October, in the chic Marais district. Nearby, someone had sprayed “mort aux riches” across the window of a bank.

The previous weekend, Paris had been rocked by mass demonstrations that in some areas had escalated into riots and looting. Further demonstrations, highlighting the neglected state of France’s secondary schools, the ever-rising cost of living and other grievances, had been planned in Paris and other French cities on the afternoon of Saturday 24 October. Unemployment in France for those aged 15 to 24 currently stands at 21.5%, almost three times the rate in neighbouring Germany.

On Tuesday 20 October, the day of the ultra-exclusive Avant-Première pre-preview of Art Basel Paris in the Grand Palais, the French activist collective Pillage de Classe (class plunder) posted a message on Instagram exhorting protesters to “take back” the famous Belle Époque exhibition hall on Saturday, the penultimate day of the week’s flagship fair.

Art Basel Paris has been held in the historic Grand Palais since 2024.

According to recent reports, of course, the Grand Palais was not stormed, Bastille-style. In the highly unlikely event of protesters managing to “take back” the building, they would have been disappointed, just as revolutionaries had been in 1789, when they discovered the prison they had liberated contained just seven detainees. Art Basel Paris, taking no risks, had closed the event two days early on Friday evening (after an excoriating letter from France's gallery association to fair director Karim Crippa, Art Basel recompensed exhibitors 20% of their stand fees).

In a recent development, the mega-gallery Hauser & Wirth took even fewer risks, emptying its stand the day before, leaving three paintings by the local artist Hélène Delprat. The fair had been shortened to three VIP preview days plus just one day for the general public. Satellite fairs, like Paris Internationale and Post-Fair, closed at lunchtime on Saturday.

That Saturday afternoon, more than 100,000 people duly turned out to demonstrate. However, these proved predominantly peaceful and were confined by the police to the outskirts of the city.

In a recent development, the disruption in Paris had surely been a momentary blip. And Art Basel’s ultra-wealthy invitees, which the top end of the international art trade likes to call the “right kind of people”, had already been and gone. But what about the reputational impact?

“The collateral damage is substantial considering the whole point of being in Paris is to let yourself surrender to its myriad charms,” noted Andrew Terner, a Fresh York-based private dealer and collector, speaking in the immediate aftermath of the early closure.

The French authorities blamed “ultra-left radical groups” for the violence that had marred weeks of otherwise peaceful protests, begun in September by discontented teenage lycée students. Pillage de Classe is certainly a left-wing radical group; it views Art Basel Paris as a luxury playground in which art is used by the ultra-wealthy to protect their capital from taxation.

It has been revealed that but maybe (leaving aside its desire to take the Grand Palais by storm) Pillage de Classe has a point, at least with regard to the fair’s top French clients. In France, the net worth of the country’s 500 wealthiest individuals has ballooned from 6% of the country’s GDP in 1996 to 42% in 2024, according to a much-cited article in the French business magazine Challenges. Tax reforms introduced by President Macron in 2017 excluded stocks, financial assets (including art) and corporate investments from wealth tax calculations.

Moreover, in 2003 the French government had granted tax breaks of up to 75% for private individuals and 60% for corporations that supported the arts. This encouraged investment in glitzy private foundations, such as the Fondation Louis Vuitton, François Pinault’s Bourse de Commerce, the Fondation Cartier and the newly opened Île Seguin luxury hotel and Large art centre, which have become such an alluring feature of the Paris art scene for international visitors. According to research by Apollo magazine, Bernard Arnault’s LVMH luxury group received an aggregate tax break of €518.1m between 2007 and 2017 to set against the €790m the corporation spent building the Frank Gehry-designed Fondation Louis Vuitton.

The ultra-wealthy have also grown a lot wealthier in the US in recent years. The share of the nation’s wealth held by the richest 0.0001% (around 200 individuals) is now more than seven times what it was in 1980, according to a November Substack posted by the Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman.

According to recent reports, today’s art market is dominated by the world’s wealthiest people buying the world’s most expensive art. Most of these people are pretty old. This is not a good look now that the Democrats have won a landslide victory in the US midterm elections, driven by a massive turnout of young voters. Authoritarian rulers like Viktor Orbán in Hungary and Aleksandar Vučić in Serbia have been voted out of office. Young people have been protesting en masse about their diminished life chances in France and more than a dozen other countries across the world.

Sources indicate that suddenly, ordinary people matter again. The young matter. But do they matter at art fairs?

Industry observers note that take ticket-pricing. In October, the general public were charged £48 each to attend Frieze London, with students being asked to pay £32. Does Frieze, which is owned by the billionaire Ari Emanuel, the former chief executive of the US entertainment conglomerate Endeavor, want to actively discourage young people from visiting? Or is that ticket price an acknowledgement that pretty much the only students who can now afford to attend the UK’s art colleges come from more affluent backgrounds?

The following week, Art Basel Paris, part of James Murdoch’s Lupa Systems investment portfolio, was charging €47 for a standard day pass and €30 for a student ticket. “The galleries pay for the fair. Visitors are a side business,” states Magnus Resch, a Upcoming York-based author and art market entrepreneur. According to Resch’s back-of-an-envelope calculations, stand fees generate at least €15m, while tickets bring in less than €3m. “Charging the public €47 isn’t about the money. It’s about keeping the fair exclusive.” (Art Basel does not reveal detailed breakdowns of its revenue streams.).

“It is notable for the public to visit an art fair,” says Guillaume Sultana, whose contemporary art gallery exhibited on the upper level of Art Basel Paris, where footfall is slower than down on the ground floor among the mega-galleries. “But a lot of general visitors on the weekend are a bit frustrated because public tickets are very expensive.”.

According to recent reports, sultana acknowledges that “the main business is done during the very first days of an art fair, always”. Despite the fair being truncated, Sultana describes the experience as “very good”, having sold a painting by the young Syrian artist Osama Al Rayyan during the preview for €15,000, among other works.

In a recent development, in the funfair-mirror optics of the international art market, €15,000 might appear a relatively “affordable” price point. But traditionally, sensible collectors have been advised to spend no more than 5% of their available wealth on art. So, whoever bought that Al Rayan painting, should, theoretically, have had €300,000 of spare cash available. For would-be younger collectors in today’s tough economic conditions, these are intimidating figures, unless they can call on the bank of mum and dad.

According to recent reports, collecting art is in serious danger of being perceived as something that old, rich people do. With so many established collectors ageing and selling, rather than buying, and a democratic wave pushing back against oligarchical wealth, this might be a good moment for the art market to think more about inclusivity than exclusivity, to take a broader view of who might be the “right kind” of people.

After all, who wants “death to the rich” sprayed across their gallery window?

How to Start a Side Business While Working Full-Time

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2253 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy.
  • Validation does not require a perfect product.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The number one reason side businesses fail is not lack of funding, bad timing, or tough competition — it is building something nobody wants to buy. Before you spend a dollar on a website, business cards, or inventory, you need to validate that real people will pay real money for what you are offering.

Validation does not require a perfect product. It requires proof of demand. Talk to 10 people who match your target customer. Describe what you blueprint to offer. Ask two questions: "Would you pay for this?" and "How much would you pay?" If 3 or more say yes with a specific dollar amount, you have a viable idea. If most say "that sounds cool" but hesitate on paying, you have a hobby.

The FI community has a particular advantage here. Many FI seekers have already cut their expenses to the point where a side business does not need to generate massive revenue to make a meaningful impact. Even $500 to $1,000 per month in side business income — invested consistently — can shave years off your FI timeline.

According to recent reports, forget building a $1 million business. Your only goal is reaching $1,000 in total revenue as rapidly as possible. That first $1,000 proves three things: people will pay you, you can deliver, and the business model works. Everything after $1,000 is optimization. The FI community calls this the "ramen profitable" stage — your business covers its own costs and generates even a small surplus. From there, you compound both your skills and your revenue.

Recent findings suggest that side business income is the ultimate FI accelerator because it attacks both sides of the equation. Your day job covers expenses while 100% of your side income goes directly to investments. If your side business generates $1,500 per month and you invest all of it at 7% annual returns, you will have over $450,000 in 15 years. That is not a theoretical number — that is the real math of why thousands of FI seekers build side businesses.

One of the first decisions you face is how to structure your business legally. For most side businesses, the choice is between operating as a sole proprietorship (the default — no paperwork needed) or forming an LLC (Limited Liability Tech giant). Here is the honest comparison.

According to recent reports, A sole proprietorship is what you are by default when you start earning money on the side. There is no registration required at the federal level (though you may need a local business license). The income flows directly to your personal tax return on Schedule C. The downside: your personal assets — savings, home equity, investments — are not separated from business liabilities.

An LLC creates a legal separation between you and your business. If someone sues your business, your personal assets are generally protected. Formation costs range from $50 (states like Kentucky and Colorado) to $500 (California charges $800 per year just for the privilege of having an LLC). For most side businesses, an LLC is worth forming once you have paying customers.

Side business income is taxed differently than your W-2 paycheck, and the surprises can be painful if you are not prepared.

Industry observers note that self-employment tax: You pay both the employee AND employer portions of Social Security and Medicare — a combined 15.3% on top of your income tax. On W-2 income, your employer covers half. On side business income, you cover it all.

Industry observers note that quarterly estimated taxes: The IRS expects you to pay taxes as you earn, not once a year in April. If you owe more than $1,000 in taxes from side business income, you need to file quarterly estimated payments (Form 1040-ES) by April 15, June 15, September 15, and January 15.

Deductions that reduce your tax bill: Home office (simplified method: $5/sq ft up to 300 sq ft = $1,500 deduction), internet (business percentage), equipment, software subscriptions, mileage ($0.76 per mile in 2027), health insurance premiums (if self-employed), and retirement contributions (Solo 401k allows up to $75,000/year). These deductions are a significant FI advantage because they reduce both income tax AND self-employment tax.

Ready to unlock a world of free travel? Start with the Chase Sapphire Preferred® Card.

It has been revealed that the biggest constraint for side business owners is not money — it is time. You have 168 hours per week. Your day job takes 40-50. Sleep takes 49-56. That leaves 62-79 hours for everything else: family, health, friends, and your business. The key is not finding more time. It is being ruthlessly strategic about the time you have.

It has been revealed that the 5-5-2 Framework: Dedicate 5 hours per weeknight (after work), 5 hours on Saturday, and 2 hours on Sunday to your business during the launch phase. That is 12 hours per week — enough to build meaningful momentum without destroying your health or relationships. After launch, you can often reduce to 5-8 hours per week for maintenance.

According to recent reports, batch your work. Do not context-switch between your day job and side business throughout the day. Dedicate specific blocks of time to specific tasks: Monday and Wednesday evenings for content creation, Tuesday and Thursday for customer communication, Saturday morning for strategic work.

The FI community offers a unique perspective on this question. Traditional business advice states to go full-time when your side income replaces your salary. The FI approach is more nuanced: your side business does not need to replace your income if your investments are covering the gap.

Consider going full-time when your side business income covers at least 75% of your essential expenses for 6 consecutive months, you have 12 months of expenses in cash reserves, your business is growing (not plateauing), and you have health insurance figured out independently of your employer.

But here is the FI twist: many people in the community deliberately keep their side business as a side business forever. A day job provides steady income, benefits, and 401(k) matching, while the side business provides additional investment capital. This "two-income engine" approach can cut your FI timeline dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses and your side business generates $2,000 per month in investable income, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years at 7% returns.

The decision depends on your personal FI strategy. Some people want to build a business that replaces their job and provides fulfillment in early retirement. Others want to maximize total income during their accumulation phase and retire from everything. Both are valid paths — the crucial thing is making the choice intentionally with the math in front of you.

From idea to first dollar with minimal risk.

Talk to 10 people who match your target customer profile. Describe your offer and ask if they would pay, and how much. Get at least 3 verbal commitments before building anything. If you cannot find 3 out of 10, pivot your idea.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Pre-sell before you build. Create a simple landing page describing your product or service and see if people will put down a deposit or join a waitlist.

Open a separate business bank account (free at most banks). File for an LLC in your state if you are ready for revenue. Get an EIN from the IRS (free, takes 5 minutes online). Set aside 30% of every dollar earned for taxes.

Sources indicate that pro tip: Do not commingle business and personal finances. A separate bank account makes tax time dramatically easier and protects your LLC liability shield.

Create the simplest version of your product or service that delivers value. A consultant needs a one-page website and a Calendly link. A product business needs one SKU, not twenty. A freelancer needs a portfolio with three examples. Launch ugly and improve based on real customer feedback.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Spend less than $200 on your MVP. If you need to spend more, you are overbuilding before you have proven demand.

Your first customers will come from your personal network, not from marketing. Tell everyone you know what you are building. Offer a founding-member discount in exchange for detailed feedback and a testimonial. The goal is revenue and learning, not profit.

Pro tip: Ask every customer two questions after delivery: "What was the best part?" and "What would you change?" These answers shape your product roadmap.

Once you have proven the model works, build systems so the business runs efficiently. Create templates, automate invoicing, document your processes. Find the acquisition channel that produces the best customers (referrals, content marketing, paid ads) and double down on it.

It has been revealed that pro tip: Track your effective hourly rate. If you earn $1,000 in a month and spend 20 hours, your rate is $50/hour. If you spend 80 hours, it is $12.50/hour — below minimum wage. Optimize for $/hour, not just total revenue.

According to recent reports, the most powerful FI strategy is not choosing between your day job and a side business — it is running both simultaneously. Your day job covers all living expenses, employer benefits, and 401(k) matching. Your side business generates pure investment capital. If your side business produces $2,000 per month and you invest every dollar at 7% annual returns, you add over $700,000 to your portfolio in 15 years. That is the difference between retiring at 55 and retiring at 45.

Check your employment contract and company handbook for non-compete clauses, moonlighting policies, and intellectual property agreements. Many employers have no policy against side businesses as long as they do not compete, use company resources, or interfere with your job performance. If your contract has restrictions, consult an employment attorney before launching. Transparency is usually the safest approach if your side business is in a completely different industry.

It has been revealed that most service-based side businesses can launch for under $200: a domain name ($12/year), basic website hosting ($5-$15/month), and a business bank account (free). Product businesses may need $500-$2,000 for initial inventory. The FI approach is to minimize upfront investment and validate before spending. If your idea requires $10,000+ to test, consider whether there is a simpler version you can launch first.

Sources indicate that businesses with flexible hours and no geographic constraints work best: freelance writing, web development, consulting in your area of expertise, online tutoring, bookkeeping, virtual assistance, and digital product creation (courses, templates, ebooks). The key criteria are: work can be done on your schedule, no physical storefront needed, and revenue can grow without proportional time investment.

Report all income on Schedule C of your personal tax return. Pay self-employment tax (15.3%) plus income tax on profits. File quarterly estimated taxes using Form 1040-ES if you expect to owe $1,000 or more. Deduct legitimate business expenses: home office, internet (business %), equipment, software, mileage, and health insurance premiums. Consider a Solo 401(k) to shelter up to $75,000/year from taxes — this is one of the most powerful FI tools available to self-employed individuals.

Start as a sole proprietor during the validation phase (no cost, no paperwork). Form an LLC once you have paying customers and revenue. An LLC protects your personal assets (home, savings, investments) from business lawsuits and debts. Formation costs range from $50-$500 depending on your state. California charges $800/year minimum, which may not be worth it until you are earning at least $10,000/year from the business.

Dramatically. If your day job covers all expenses at a 50% savings rate, you reach FI in about 17 years. Add $2,000/month in side business income invested entirely, and your effective savings rate jumps well above 60% — cutting your FI timeline to roughly 12-13 years. At $3,000/month side income, you could reach FI in under 10 years from starting. The key insight: side business income has nearly 100% savings rate because your day job already covers expenses.

Sources indicate that starting a side business while working full-time is one of the most powerful financial moves you can make on the path to FI. Validate your idea before spending money, set up basic legal and tax infrastructure, launch an MVP promptly, and focus relentlessly on reaching your first $1,000 in revenue. The beauty of the side business approach is that your day job covers all expenses while your business income goes directly toward building wealth. Even modest side income of $1,000 to $2,000 per month, invested consistently over 10-15 years, can add hundreds of thousands of dollars to your portfolio and cut years off your timeline to financial independence.

Single upright capitals stack cleanly from top to bottom, ending in the year 2026 at the foot. Opposite page 14, Omnitypeâs OT Scholar takes command of the directory. Three narrow columns sort national prize winners submitted from more than thirty countries, building a competition archive that traces its Leipzig roots back to 1963 without needing a single ruled divider line. Winners get solid black numbered dots. Fourteen awardees, led by Dutch Goldene Letter recipient Ouroboros Wings, French Gold Medal winner Picalso, and Silver Medal titles Odes and Sophie Thun: Zwischen Licht und Wand, carry white numerals inside black discs â while shortlisted books below wear hollow hairline rings.

That three-column grid holds steady across every country section, from Belgium and Canada to China, Austria, and Hungary. Inside each narrow column, left-aligned roman labels for Title, Author/Editor, Publisher, Design, Illustration/Photography, Printer, and ISBN hang clean beside italic book titles and thirteen-digit numbers. Dense Hungarian, Czech, and German diacritics stay sharp even at compact catalog sizes. Whenever a listed book wins a medal, its numbered black dot and jury commentary drop right inline above paired monochrome object photos anchored at the lower margin. Faint show-through across the thin uncoated pages gives this book design catalog the quiet utility of a working Leipzig Book Fair reference.

When It Makes Sense To “Block” The Main Thread

📅 2026-07-17 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2062 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that I Code.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that I Code. I Write. Meme Rules. Ok, but seriously, I’m a web and mobile developer who writes a lot. In my spare time, I like to build products that would … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve all heard of the sacred rule in modern web development, the rule never to be broken. The rule of “Never block the main thread.”.

You almost can’t miss it as a web developer; it’s in almost every performance guide, and to be fair, it is good advice. We all know the browser’s main thread is single-threaded, meaning it can only do one thing at a time.

Industry observers note that plus, as we know, the main thread isn’t ours alone; we share it with the browser’s rendering engine, input handlers, and other critical tasks. As a result, the less time we hold onto the main thread, the more responsive an app feels. That leads us to share tasks with background workers as we’ve convinced ourselves there should be a hard line between the UI and any computation, and that line shouldn’t be crossed.

And that is what a “recommended” architecture looks like.

But I dare say that *sometimes*, moving the data to a worker is slower than just letting the main thread do the work.

In a recent development, I found this out a few months ago while building a Chrome extension with screenshotting features called Fastary. I kept finding a latency of about 2 to 3 seconds in all my testing, even after using an Offscreen Document (a background process in Chrome extensions) to handle the canvas operations. A screenshot task should feel instant without lag, after all.

Sources indicate that it is quite ironic that by reflex, we move work away from the main thread to avoid freezing the UI, but sometimes the act of moving that work (e.g., serializing, copying, and deserializing) can also freeze the UI. And sometimes the recommended approach of letting the background do the work can be slower than just doing the work on the main thread.

To put things in perspective, let’s understand why we isolate browser contexts and how they communicate with each other, with emphasis on the communication part.

A browser is more than a single environment. Different environments are running at the same time, each having its own memory space, what it can access, and rules:.

Each one of these is isolated from the others. A web worker or background script lives in a different memory space from the main thread. They cannot just reach and read each other’s variables or logic, and this is known as the “shared-nothing” architecture.

How do these isolated environments communicate? They explicitly message each other back and forth using APIs, like postMessage().

postMessage() tells the browser to take a piece of data and deliver it to the context that requested it. But to do this, the browser relies on the Structured Clone Algorithm (SCA).

You’re probably familiar with JSON.stringify(). SCA is similar, but much stronger and smarter. In its simplest form, SCA is a deep, recursive copy operation, i.e., cloning. It walks through the entire data structure it is given, clones every single value, serializes it into a transportable format, ships those bytes to the target contexts, and then reconstructs the original object on the receiving side.

SCA is fast, or maybe fast-ish… For a small regular config object like {theme: "dark"}, it is imperceptible; you don’t even notice it. The story changes, however, when dealing with heavy data because the SCA is a synchronous blocking O(n) operation, i.e., the cost increases linearly with the size of your data.

In a recent development, let’s put that into perspective. A user clicks a button, and internally, an 8MB image payload is sent to a background worker for processing. When you call postMessage(), the main thread must immediately stop what it is doing to run this serialization and copying process.

I’m sure some of you are already thinking, “Why not just use Transferable objects?” And that is a valid point. Let’s talk about that.

Developers who really pursue ultra-high-performance web apps usually use Transferable objects (e.g., ArrayBuffer, ImageBitmap, or MessagePort) to bypass the Structured Clone Algorithm. This is because when you transfer an object, you’re not making a copy (like SCM). Instead, the browser switches ownership of the data from one context to another.

Recent findings suggest that the browser performs a hand-off whereby the sending context loses access to the data instantly, and the receiving context takes full control. It is actually insanely fast. According to Chrome Developers’ benchmark, transferring a massive 32MB ArrayBuffer can take under 7ms, compared to about 300ms when cloning with SCM. That’s a 43x speed boost.

Industry observers note that but like all good things, there are downsides. To name a few:.

So, as far as my screenshot extension went, Transferable objects were not an option.

Why do we even bother isolating contexts at all? Why not just leave it all to the main thread?

According to recent reports, offloading long-running CPU tasks to a background thread is absolutely the right thing to do. The browser needs to paint a new frame every 16.6ms to keep things fluid; that means any task that takes >50ms is generally considered “long”. Offloading to the background is absolutely the right thing to do.

The glitch, however, is that we’ve turned this “never block the main thread” into an absolute rule, without asking is this task expensive to process or expensive to move?

I have come to realize now that the rule is less “never block the main thread” than “never block the main thread for too long.”.

My goal with the Fastary extension was to make it feel like a native app, running as smoothly and instantly as you would expect a native app to.

According to recent reports, as you already know, I took the recommended approach to use the Offscreen Document to handle DOM work in the background. But to my surprise, that took a different turn.

It has been revealed that the Offscreen Document API is a clear winner. You create a hidden, undisplayed document that runs entirely in the background. It has a DOM and supports Canvas. For example, if I want to crop a screenshot, stitch multiple screenshots together, perform heavy image manipulation, or add a watermark, Offscreen Document was made for that.

Turns out that was not the best approach. This was my architecture:.

Sources indicate that but when I tested it, the screenshot didn’t feel instant. As I mentioned earlier, there was a consistent 2–3 second lag.

Recent findings suggest that I figured out that when captureVisibleTab() takes a screenshot, it returns a Base64 URL string, and on a standard 1080p screen, that string could be approximately 1MB or more, depending on how detailed the image is. It gets even more interesting on modern Retina displays (e.g., MacBooks) as they tend to automatically double the image’s size by default.

Keep in mind that since the image payload could be doubled and extension messaging relies on JSON serialization (as of this writing), we potentially deal with massive synchronous communication that costs an entire round trip.

Sources indicate that the image string data is JSON-serialized at least twice: once when going into the Offscreen Document and once coming back out with the processed results to the background worker. The actual image processing (cropping) done inside the Offscreen Document was fast, no doubt, but I can’t say the same about the transfer overhead.

Sources indicate that as if the latency itself wasn’t enough, I noticed a rather subtle bug — which, now that I think of it, was more of my ignorance. After a screenshot was taken, the crop result was completely off in a way that either weirdly scaled the image or resulted in incorrect coordinates.

It turns out that when a user selects a region to crop, the content script gets the box coordinates using getBoundingClientRect(), which is measured in CSS pixels; this is what the DOM uses. But when the screenshot is captured natively in Chrome, the browser doesn’t crop it automatically; it instead uses the physical hardware pixels to get the full screen capture. And the browser uses devicePixelRatio (DPR) to know how many physical pixels should represent one CSS pixel. Basically, if a user on a Retinal display (DPR = 2) highlights an area of 400x300 CSS pixels, the actual captured image area is 800x600 physical pixels.

For an accurate crop, I needed to apply these two different measurement systems with the right DPR, i.e., scale the crop coordinates by the DPR. But remember, Offscreen Documents have no physical display. Processing any image would have a default DPR equal to 1. To fix this, I would have to capture the exact devicePixelRatio from the active tab, serialize it, pass it alongside the image payload, and manually do the scaling math inside the Offscreen Document. The complexity starts to compound.

What if I broke the golden rule and did the work on the main thread instead?

It has been revealed that some developers will argue that UI tasks are the only things that should run on the main thread, but I don’t fully agree with that. Personally, I believe that user explicitly-invoked actions that need immediate results can sometimes get a solid pass to run on the main thread, provided the work is incredibly fast (e.g., 1s).

That’s what I did: scrap out the Offscreen Document and reengineer the logic. Instead of:.

…I decided to run the whole image processing in the active tab:.

This approach completely clears out multiple context hops and round trips that JSON serialization requires. The only cross-context transfer involves sending the data URL from the background to the content script.

The Retina DPI concern essentially solved itself, as the content script runs directly inside the real, active browser tab because it knows the monitor’s real devicePixelRatio.

But there’s an elephant in the room that you may have noticed.

According to recent reports, sure, the image is now processed on the main thread, and the background manipulates the canvas in the active tab. I could technically be blocking the main thread. That’s where I amended the “no blocking the main thread” rule to “no blocking the main thread for too long.” In this specific case, at least, blocking the main thread for a task the user requests for approximately one second is justifiable. It works conversely as well: maybe don’t isolate processes if the data transfer cost is greater than the processing cost.

I’ve boiled it down to a mental model that depends on whether the task is:.

It has been revealed that these are tasks where the primary cost is computation and not the size of the data itself. These are tasks where most of the time is spent on doing calculations or heavy transformations, e.g., image compression, audio profiling, physics simulation, etc.

The transfer cost for these tasks is minuscule compared to the actual work.

These tasks are the exact opposite. These tasks are only expensive because of the size. The processing time is almost insignificant, but the data is expensive to transport, e.g., image cropping, filtering an array, shallow copy, etc.

In my specific case, offloading the task to the background falls mostly into negative-sum efficiency. If we are talking about moving megabytes of data to perform a 50ms operation, there is no benefit to offloading it to the background.

Perhaps we can think of it like this:.

Recent findings suggest that looking at this, if the “background processing time” is the most dominant task in your operation, then isolation is the clear winner. But if serialization, plus deserialization, plus transit exceeds that cost, then there’s no need to isolate things.

And if you can’t figure out if the task is CPU-heavy or data-heavy, it certainly doesn’t hurt to measure it, for example, using performance.mark() and performance.measure() around postMessage calls to profile the transfer cost.
